title: Radio Basics
summary: Use basic radio knowledge to listen for alerts, conserve power, and make a clear distress call.

sections.heading: Step 1 — Know common emergency radio types
sections.body: NOAA weather radios can receive hazard alerts in supported regions and are often useful for storms and other emergencies. Amateur radio, or ham radio, is widely used by trained operators for long-distance and local emergency communication. FRS and GMRS radios are simple handheld options for short-range use where permitted by local law.
sections.image_description: A row of different handheld radios labeled weather, ham, and short-range.

sections.heading: Step 2 — Listen for distress and emergency channels
sections.body: Marine distress calling often uses channel 16 at 156.8 MHz, and aviation distress historically uses 121.5 MHz for emergency monitoring. In any emergency, follow local rules and established radio procedures for the specific service you are using. Listening first is often the best way to learn what channel is active for help.
sections.image_description: A radio display showing 156.8 MHz and 121.5 MHz with a distress icon.

sections.heading: Step 3 — Make a clear distress call
sections.body: Keep the message short and structured: who you are, where you are, what is happening, and what help you need. Speak slowly and repeat the most important information if necessary. If a radio operator responds, follow their instructions exactly and stay on the channel unless told otherwise.
sections.warning: Do not clutter a distress channel with unnecessary speech.
sections.image_description: A sample distress call format card with location, problem, and help needed.

sections.heading: Step 4 — Save battery and improve reception
sections.body: Reduce transmit power when close to the receiver and keep transmissions brief to conserve battery. Turn the radio off when not needed and lower screen or backlight use if the device has one. A simple improvised antenna or moving to higher ground can sometimes improve reception, but use only safe, legal methods.
sections.image_description: A battery icon, low-power symbol, and a simple wire antenna sketch.

when_to_use: Use this guide when you need to receive emergency information or send a distress message by radio.
do_not: Do not assume every frequency is monitored everywhere.
Do not drain batteries with long transmissions.
Do not transmit outside the rules for your radio service.
